message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This study is built on a six-month pilot with 4,000 households across three deliberately mixed wards, so the projections are based on how Thornbury residents actually behave, not national averages. We measured participation and tonnage weekly, by housing type, and the results are encouraging: strong participation, consistent yields and 81% of residents rating the service good or very good. Crucially, participation held up across houses and flats, which means we can roll out a single, simple service across the district rather than designing separate arrangements. The financial analysis is complete and transparent. Every cost line is shown, from vehicles to liners, and the disposal saving uses our actual incineration cost and Brookfield's quoted gate fee, giving a net cost of about £490,000 that is fully covered by the provisional new-burdens allocation. Treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away. The timetable works back from the vehicle lead time. I am confident the Council can approve this roll-out knowing it is evidence-based and fully funded.
</author>

<document>
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.
</document>
response:
# Review: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection Feasibility Study

The arithmetic in Table 2 is correct. However, three problems in the pilot data and treatment section undermine the two main conclusions: that a uniform service works for houses and flats, and that the service is fully funded. As written, I don't think Cabinet could safely approve on this basis.

## Major issues

### 1. Flats did not participate at a similar rate to houses

Table 1 shows **66% participation for houses and 21% for flats**, three times lower. Section 2 says participation was "broadly similar across housing types," and Section 7 recommends a uniform service on that basis. The data shows the opposite: the standard caddy service did not work well for flats.

About 10,400 of the district's 52,000 households are flats, so this matters. The study should acknowledge the gap and consider a flats-specific approach, such as communal bins, different bin-store arrangements or targeted communications. It should also cost that approach, which will add to Table 2.

### 2. The projection uses a participation rate that isn't in the pilot

Section 3 applies a **64%** participation rate, but the pilot's overall rate was **57%** (2,280 ÷ 4,000). The 3,290-tonne figure follows from 64%, so it is overstated.

The pilot's housing mix (20% flats) matches the district's, so the pilot rates can be applied directly by housing type:

| | Households | Participation | kg/week | Tonnes/year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 66% | 1.9 | ~2,713 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 21% | 1.4 | ~159 |
| **Total** | 52,000 | | | **~2,870** |

That is about **420 tonnes (13%) lower** than the study's figure. The "All" yield of 1.9 kg is also slightly rounded up; the weighted figure is about 1.86 kg.

### 3. Brookfield cannot take the projected tonnage

Section 4 says Brookfield can offer **up to 1,800 tonnes a year until 2029**. Both the study's 3,290 t and the corrected ~2,870 t exceed this, by 1,490 t and ~1,070 t respectively. The study doesn't address this. As a result:

- The £243,000 saving assumes every tonne goes to Brookfield at £38. Only 1,800 t can, which is worth £133,200 at £74/t.
- The remaining ~1,070 t would have to go to the plant 46 miles away. Its gate fee is unknown, and the study includes no costs for haulage, transfer or extra vehicle time.
- "Treatment is local" is true for only about 60–65% of the tonnage, and only until 2029.
- Brookfield has said it "can offer" capacity. The study should say whether a contract or heads of terms are in place.

## Effect on the funding conclusion

| | Study | Corrected tonnage, all at Brookfield rates | Brookfield capacity limit applied |
|---|---|---|---|
| Disposal saving | £243,000 | ~£212,500 | £133,200 + unknown result on ~1,070 t |
| Net cost | ~£490,000 | ~£521,000 | **≥ ~£600,000** plus haulage/second-plant costs |
| vs £520,000 allocation | Covered | Slightly over | **Not covered** |

Even the middle column, which is optimistic, exceeds the allocation. This is before any flats-specific provision is added.

The allocation is also described as **provisional**, and the Government has only "indicated" that funding will be provided. "Fully funded" in Section 7 should be qualified. The study should state when the allocation will be confirmed and what happens if it comes in lower.

## Other points

- **Cost completeness.** Table 2 omits several items:
  - spare vehicle capacity (six vehicles, none spare)
  - cover for crew absence and leave
  - supervision and depot costs
  - the launch phone line
  - all costs of delivering to the second AD plant

  Please state whether the £34,000 per operative includes on-costs. Ongoing liners appear to fall within the £88,000 "annualised" line. A breakdown would support the "every cost line shown" claim.
- **Pilot trends.** Only six-month averages are reported, though data was collected weekly. Including the trend, particularly whether participation declined over the period, would strengthen the projection.
- **Satisfaction figure.** The 81% is of "surveyed" households. Give the sample size and response rate, and say whether non-participants were included. A survey that mainly reached participants would overstate satisfaction.
- **Timetable.** The vehicle order deadline is December 2026, with a four-month lead time. The study should note that Cabinet approval is needed almost immediately and say what the fallback is if delivery slips past March 2027. Contracted treatment capacity also needs to be secured before the April start.

## Suggested changes before submission

1. Correct the Section 2 statement on flats, drop "uniform" from the recommendation, and set out and cost a flats approach.
2. Re-run the projection using the pilot rates by housing type (~2,870 t).
3. Add a treatment plan for tonnage above Brookfield's 1,800 t, with costs, and confirm the contractual status with Brookfield.
4. Recalculate the net cost and present it against the provisional allocation, with a sensitivity range and a funding-gap scenario.
5. Complete the cost lines listed above.

The pilot provides a good evidence base, and the core house-based service looks viable. The study's conclusions just need to match what the evidence shows.
